newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: ABARE cuts 1997 gold price forecast to US$352/oz.
newsitem.headline: ABARE cuts 1997 gold price forecast to US$352/oz.

text.p: The Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) on Tuesday cut its 1997 forecast for gold to US$352 an ounce from US$375.

"Recent announcements by the Swiss and German central banks have sustained market uncertainty about future gold sales by the European official sector, which emerged in 1996," ABARE said in its latest commodities outlook report.
Average prices received by Australian gold miners also are expected to suffer, declining to an average A$456 an ounce in 1997 from A$497 in 1996, ABARE said.
Australia's gold production, meanwhile, is set to rise 7.2 percent to 319 tonnes in 1997/98 (July-June) from the previous year, ABARE said.
The forecast takes into account a decline in gold output in the March quarter to an estimated 72.5 tonnes, down two tonnes from the previous quarter, owing to adverse weather at some mine sites.
In its earlier forecast, ABARE put 1997/98 gold production at 320 tonnes.
Australia's gold yield is forecast to increase to around 78 tonnes a quarter over the rest of 1997/98 despite recent declines in the gold price and prospects of higher mining costs, ABARE said.
Australia's weighted average industry cash cost of production is estimated to have increased to US$282 an ounce in calendar 1996 from US$262 in 1995, ABARE said.

"When compared with estimates of other countries' cash costs by Gold Fields Mineral Sevices Ltd, these figures reveal Australia to be the second highest cost producer in U.S. dollar terms in the world after South Africa," ABARE said.
The upward cost trend also reflects a continuing structural shift in the Australian industry from small-scale open pit mining to larger-scale open pit and underground mining, it said.
Australian exports of gold should rise 6.3 percent in 1997/98 to over 356 tonnes, reflecting strong growth in domestic production, ABARE said.
Increased gold refining capacity in neighbouring countries to Australia, such as Papua New Guinea and Indonesia, would limit growth potential in exports of gold of overseas origin, ABARE said.

Still, a forecast modest rise in the U.S. dollar gold price later this year and higher export volumes are expected to result in the value of Australian gold exports increasing 7.2 percent in 1997/98 to A$5.385 billion, ABARE said.
ABARE pinned a global slump in the gold price so far in 1997 to uncertainty among investors about any future gold sales by European central banks.

The gold market was first rattled in February when the Swiss National Bank announced a plan to establish a fund for victims of the Holocaust by selling between 400 and 840 tonnes of gold over 10 years.
Shortly after, Germany's Bundesbank said it was studying a propsal to revalue around 3,700 tonnes of its gold reserves.
Nevertheless, an expanding rise in demand from the jewellery sector over mine production should place a floor price on gold in the near term and over the medium term push up the price, ABARE said.
Some tightening of scrap supplies can also be expected in the wake of current price levels, it said.

"On balance, the timing and extent of any upturn in prices from the recent low trading range (US$340-US$350 an ounce) over the course of 1997 will depend largely on the actvities and pronouncements of European central banks in the next few months," ABARE said.
Reflecting the uncertainty in the market, the 1997 average price forecast is likely to have a 75 percent probability of being in a range of US$337 to US$357 an ounce, ABARE said.
